# Classification of Living Organisms

Imagine you have a huge library with thousands of books, but there are no labels on the shelves. Finding the exact story you want would be impossible. Nature is similar. There are millions of different living things on Earth, from tiny ants to giant elephants. To make sense of this vast variety, scientists group them into categories. This grouping is called classification. Classification helps us understand the relationships between different living things and makes studying them much easier.

## The Need for Classification

The Earth is full of life, from large trees and shrubs to small insects, and even tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye. All these living beings, along with the places where they live, make up the biosphere. The biosphere includes land, water, and air, where life interacts with its surroundings to survive and grow. Scientists need a system to organize these millions of species. Without classification, keeping track of all the different plants and animals would be a complete mess. By sorting them into groups, scientists can easily study how they live, what they eat, and how they grow.

## The Hierarchy of Groups

To classify living things, scientists use a system of levels called a hierarchy. Think of it like a set of nested boxes. The biggest box is the kingdom, and inside it are smaller boxes like phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. The smallest box is the species.

A species is a group of living things that can breed with each other and produce young. For example, all dogs belong to the same species, *Canis lupus familiaris*. A genus is a group of closely related species. For example, tigers and lions belong to the same genus, *Panthera*. A family is a group of closely related genera. An order is a group of related families. A class is a group of related orders. A phylum is a group of related classes. Finally, a kingdom is the largest group, containing many different phyla.

## Levels of Organisation in an Organism

To understand how complex living things are built, we can look at the levels of organisation inside a single body. The body of a living organism is organised in a complex way. The basic unit of life is the cell, just like a brick is the basic unit of a wall. A group of similar cells forms a type of tissue. Different tissues are organised to form an organ. Several organs work together to form an organ system that performs a major function of the body. All the organ systems together make up a complete organism—like a plant or an animal.

The levels of organisation are:
Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism

These levels of organisation help us understand how simple building blocks like cells come together to form a complex living being. The life of complex living organisms begins with a single cell—‘egg’. The egg of any organism has an amazing ability to divide repeatedly to form a complete living being made up of many cells. Such living beings are called multicellular organisms. Animals, including humans, and plants are all examples of multicellular organisms.

## Worked Example

Let us apply the hierarchy rule to a common animal. Suppose we want to classify the tiger. The tiger belongs to the species *Panthera tigris*. The genus is *Panthera*. The family is Felidae, which includes cats, lions, and tigers. The order is Carnivora, which includes meat-eating animals. The class is Mammalia, which includes all mammals. The phylum is Chordata, which includes animals with a spinal cord. The kingdom is Animalia, which includes all animals.

## Key points
*   Classification is the grouping of living organisms to understand their relationships and make them easier to study.
*   The hierarchy of classification groups living things from the largest group, kingdom, to the smallest group, species.
*   The levels of organisation in a multicellular organism are: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism.
*   All complex living organisms, including humans and plants, are multicellular, meaning they are made up of many cells.
*   The biosphere includes all living beings and the places where they live, such as land, water, and air.
